name: proxy
intent: Provide a stand-in object with the same interface as the real subject that interposes on every access, so that access can be controlled, deferred or recorded without changing the subject or its clients.
problem: Access to an object must pass through policy - creation deferred until first use, permission checks, caching or logging, reference counting, or a different address space - but neither the subject nor its callers should be modified, and callers should not have to know which policy is in force. Hard-wiring the policy into the subject couples it to one concern; hard-wiring it into every caller duplicates it.
context: Applies when a client depends on an object through an interface or class that cannot or should not change, and the access path itself is the right home for the policy: heavyweight resources created on demand, sensitive operations needing authorization, results worth caching, subjects living in another process, or objects whose lifetime must be tracked. It is a reference-semantics, per-object decision - the proxy stands in for one subject, or for one family of subjects behind a shared interface.
benefits: Control is centralized on the access path: authorization, validation, logging, caching and admission checks run once in the proxy instead of in every caller or in the subject itself.
Clients and subject stay untouched - both depend only on the shared interface, so a proxy can be inserted or removed without editing either side (Open/Closed).
Expensive subjects can be deferred or shared: virtual proxies create on demand, copy-on-write proxies postpone copying, caching proxies reuse results.
The proxy can own the subject's lifecycle where that helps: creation, reference counting, release and re-creation after failure are encapsulated instead of spread across callers.
Remote and protected subjects become local, ordinary objects to the client: address-space and permission details disappear behind the same calls.
A natural test seam: the proxy can record calls, inject failures or serve fixtures without touching the subject or the client.
tradeoffs: Every access pays an extra indirection - one virtual call plus the policy code; for trivial subjects this can dominate the operation it guards.
The proxy duplicates the subject's interface: every method added or changed on the subject must be mirrored, and a method added later silently bypasses the proxy until it is updated.

The policy is invisible at the call site: lazy initialization, permission checks and network round trips surface as unexplained latency or as failures far from the code that caused them, and stack traces now show a proxy frame.

Identity and equality become ambiguous: proxy and subject are different objects, so equals/hashCode, reference comparison, synchronization and collection membership can diverge unless the proxy delegates those operations deliberately.

The proxy adds failure modes of its own: lazy-initialization races and cached initialization failures, stale or unbounded caches, deadlocks when it serializes access, and dangling subjects behind remote or weak proxies.
Lifecycle ownership is easy to get wrong: a proxy that creates the subject must also destroy it, and one that outlives or is outlived by its subject either leaks or crashes.
Protection enforced only in the proxy is bypassable whenever a caller can still reach the real subject, and it can create a false sense of security.
Applied to a plain direct dependency it is pure overhead: an extra type, an extra file and an extra failure path for no policy.

participants.responsibility: Declares the common interface of the real subject and the proxy, so a proxy can be used anywhere the real subject is expected.
Defines the real object the proxy stands in for and performs the actual work once access is granted.

Holds a reference to the real subject (or the information needed to obtain it), implements the same interface, and applies its access policy - create-on-demand, permission check, cache lookup, reference counting, marshalling - before forwarding the request.
Depends only on Subject and works through the proxy without knowing whether it talks to the proxy or the real object.

use_cases: Virtual proxies: defer loading a large image, document or 3-D asset, a database connection, or a parsed configuration until first use (GoF's ImageProxy; lazy loading in ORMs like Hibernate where @Proxy(lazy=true) creates a bytecode-generated stand-in that materializes the entity on first field access).

Protection proxies: enforce authorization, capability or rate limits before a sensitive service (file system, OS object, admin API) is touched; used in enterprise Java (Spring Security), .NET and OS kernels.

Remote proxies: local stubs for objects in another process or machine - RPC clients, gRPC stubs, queue consumers - so callers write ordinary method calls while the proxy handles serialization, transport and address-space translation.

Smart references: reference-counted and copy-on-write handles that manage the subject's lifetime; C++ smart pointers (shared_ptr), Rust's Rc<Arc> and Python's weakref all exhibit smart-reference proxy behaviour.

Caching and logging proxies: memoize expensive results (e.g. YouTube video metadata fetched over network) or record and measure accesses for observability without touching the subject; HTTP CDNs are network-level caching proxies.

Circuit breakers: wrap remote service calls in a proxy that trips and fails fast when the downstream error rate exceeds a threshold, preventing cascading failures in microservices (as described in the Circuit Breaker pattern at microservices.io).

API gateways and BFF (Backends for Frontends): the single entry point in a microservices architecture acts as a proxy that routes, authenticates, rate-limits and fans out requests to appropriate backend services.

Database connection pools: a pool manager proxies raw connections; clients acquire a logical connection from the pool proxy, which internally manages physical connection reuse, health checks and eviction.

Sidecar and service mesh proxies: in cloud-native microservices (Istio/Envoy, Linkerd, Consul Connect), a sidecar proxy per pod handles mTLS, retries, circuit breaking, observability and policy enforcement without embedding logic in application code (NIST SP 800-233 sidecar model).

Python __getattr__ proxies: idiomatic Python proxies use __getattr__ for transparent delegation, functools.cached_property for attribute-level caching, and typing.Protocol for structural subtyping to type-check the proxy without inheritance.

Cloud provider SDK client proxies: AWS boto3, GCP client libraries and Azure SDK internally use service-level proxies that handle authentication, retries, pagination and endpoint resolution transparently to the caller.

Schema registry and contract proxies: proxies that intercept serialization to validate, transform or log data formats (Avro, Protobuf) at boundary crossings, ensuring schema compatibility across service versions.

Java's standard dynamic-proxy API: java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates interface-compatible stand-ins whose calls are dispatched to an InvocationHandler, giving frameworks and tests a central interception point without editing the subject.

Hibernate ORM entity proxies: org.hibernate.proxy.LazyInitializer keeps an association uninitialized until access, then resolves the entity through its session; callers use the entity abstraction while the proxy manages session-bound loading.

Istio's Envoy sidecar proxies: the data plane mediates service traffic and enforces telemetry, routing and security policy outside application code, demonstrating a deployment-level remote/protection proxy.
avoid_when: A direct reference or a plain interface extraction is enough: if no policy is interposed, the extra type is overhead.
The added behaviour is a responsibility callers should compose explicitly - use Decorator when clients choose and stack behaviours, Proxy when access itself is controlled.
The interface would have to change: that is Adapter's problem, not Proxy's.
One simple entry point over a whole subsystem is wanted: use Facade (many objects, one coarse interface).
The subject is a value with copy semantics and no shared identity: value types and copy-on-write are language features, not a proxy class.
A framework already supplies the stand-in (DI container lazy resolution, ORM lazy loading, service mesh, gRPC stubs) - configure it instead of rebuilding the structure.
anti_patterns: God proxy: one proxy that does caching, logging, authorization, retries and metrics at once, recoupling the concerns the pattern was meant to separate.

Transparent proxy that silently changes semantics: a same-interface stand-in that returns different values, swallows exceptions or mutates arguments, so callers can no longer reason about the subject's contract.
Proxy as a wrapper for a class the caller could construct directly - a layer that only forwards and never controls anything.
Bypassable protection proxy: access checks live in the proxy while the real subject remains reachable, so the policy is advisory.
Unbounded caching proxy: memoizes without eviction, turning a performance pattern into a memory leak.
Reflection proxy used where a static forwarding class or a plain interface would be clearer, hiding type errors until runtime.
Caching before authorizing: a proxy that stores results before permission checks complete, leaking protected data into the cache for unauthorized callers.
Silent failure proxy: a proxy that catches and discards exceptions or returns None on error, masking failures that callers cannot distinguish from success.
Proxy recursion: self-wiring mistake where a proxy calls itself instead of the real subject, causing stack overflow or infinite loop.
Timeout stacking: layered proxies each with their own timeouts, where outer timeouts fire before inner ones can complete, making it impossible to allocate a proper timeout budget.
design_principles: Indirection and information hiding: the proxy is the extra level of indirection that lets access policy live outside both client and subject.
Open/Closed principle: new proxies can be introduced without changing the subject or its clients.
Single responsibility: access policy in the proxy, business behaviour in the subject.
Liskov substitution: the proxy must be usable wherever the subject is expected - same interface, same observable contract, with deviations deliberate and documented.
Composition over inheritance: the proxy holds the subject rather than subclassing it; subclassing is only the interface-extraction fallback.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on the Subject abstraction, never on the concrete proxy or real subject.
best_practices: Extract or reuse the Subject interface first; only subclass the real subject when no interface can be introduced. Both the GoF pattern and Stack Overflow confirm two UML variants are valid - proxy referencing the interface (strict) or the concrete class (pragmatic) - but referencing the interface preserves Open/Closed more cleanly.

Keep the proxy's contract identical to the subject's - exceptions, nullability, side-effect order - or document the deviation as part of the type. A proxy that silently changes semantics is the Transparent Proxy anti-pattern.

Decide and document lifecycle ownership: does the proxy create the subject, share it, or receive it, and who destroys it. Hibernate's LazyInitializer and Spring's ProxyFactoryBean both require explicit lifecycle decisions.

Make lazy initialization thread-safe (OnceLock/LazyLock, Lazy<T>, sync.Once, synchronized) and decide whether a failed initialization is retried or cached. Race conditions in lazy proxies are a common source of production bugs.

Delegate identity operations (equals/hashCode/toString/comparison) deliberately; never let them silently split proxy and subject. Two objects that are logically equal (proxy == real subject) must behave consistently in sets, maps and equality checks.
Keep one policy per proxy; compose separate proxies when several concerns apply, and order them explicitly. Stacking many concerns in one god proxy recouples concerns the pattern should separate.
Give the proxy an escape hatch for tests and diagnostics (unwrap/getTarget), but keep it out of the Subject interface so production clients cannot bypass the policy.

For remote proxies, surface transport failures as declared errors and put timeouts, retries and circuit-breaking outside the subject's contract. Hiding remote latency behind a same-interface proxy without surfacing failure modes is a common source of production incidents.

Be aware of the self-invocation problem in AOP-style proxies: a method calling another method on the same object via this.foo() bypasses the proxy entirely. Spring AOP documents this explicitly; prefer self-injection or AspectJ if this matters.

Profile before adding a proxy to a hot path. Dynamic proxies (JDK's java.lang.reflect.Proxy) and CGLIB both add measurable overhead for small, frequently called methods - the relative cost is negligible for I/O-bound operations but can dominate tight compute loops.

In Python, prefer explicit forwarding over __getattr__ when static type checking, IDE autocompletion, or explicit write/__setattr__ delegation is needed; use __getattr__ for minimal, transparent delegation where runtime flexibility outweighs static clarity.

For Python typing with Protocols, remember __getattr__ bypasses static type inference; explicitly implementing delegated methods on the proxy or using a custom __getattribute__ ensures static type checkers see the correct signatures.

In cloud-native/service mesh deployments, prefer sidecar proxies (Istio Envoy, Linkerd) over application-level proxies for cross-cutting concerns (mTLS, retries, observability), keeping application code free of infrastructure wiring.

Implement explicit error mapping at proxy boundaries: translate downstream exceptions into declared error types rather than letting raw transport errors propagate, so callers see consistent error shapes.
Allocate timeout budgets intentionally in layered proxy scenarios: give each layer (proxy, transport, subject) a distinct portion of the total budget rather than stacking full timeouts at each layer.
For caching proxies, implement proper cache invalidation (TTL, event-driven eviction, size limits) and avoid caching null or error results; return them directly and fetch fresh on the next call.
In Python, use __slots__ in __getattr__-based proxies to avoid accidental attribute collisions and to prevent the proxy from acquiring its own dict, which can shadow delegated attributes.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson & Vlissides, Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software (1994) - Proxy (Structural Patterns), p. 207.

Martin Fowler, 'Lazy Load' - Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture. Describes Virtual Proxy as a lazy-loading variant with four implementation approaches (Lazy Initialization, Virtual Proxy, Value Holder, Ghost). https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/lazyLoad.html
Martin Fowler, 'Gateway' - Pattern for providing a single interface to an external system, related to Proxy in microservices contexts. https://martinfowler.com/articles/gateway-pattern.html
Martin Fowler, 'Service Stub' - Pattern for stubbing remote services in tests, a Remote Proxy variant. https://martinfowler.com/eaaCatalog/serviceStub.html

Oracle, 'Proxy' - java.lang.reflect.Proxy API documentation for Java SE, describing dynamic proxy class generation and InvocationHandler dispatch. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/reflect/Proxy.html

Spring Framework, 'Proxying Mechanisms' - Official documentation covering JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB proxy selection, proxy-target-class, @Proxyable annotation and the self-invocation problem. https://docs.spring.io/spring/reference/core/aop/proxying.html

Hibernate ORM, '@Proxy Annotation' - Official Javadoc for Hibernate's @Proxy annotation controlling lazy loading behaviour. https://docs.hibernate.org/stable/entitymanager/javadoc/org/hibernate/annotations/Proxy.html

Hibernate ORM, 'LazyInitializer' - Official Javadoc describing the interface governing Hibernate proxy initialisation, session association and read-only state. https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/current/javadocs/org/hibernate/proxy/LazyInitializer.html
Refactoring Guru, 'Proxy Design Pattern' - Comprehensive pattern description with roles, use cases and code examples in multiple languages. https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/proxy

Stack Overflow, 'How do Proxy, Decorator, Adapter and Bridge differ?' - Highly voted accepted answer (700+) clarifying intent differences between structurally similar patterns. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/350404/how-do-the-proxy-decorator-adapter-and-bridge-patterns-differ

Stack Overflow, 'Proxy Design Pattern: Association to Interface or RealSubject' - Accepted answer clarifying the two GoF UML variants and when each is appropriate. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/65740160/proxy-design-pattern-association-to-the-interface-or-realsubject

Stack Overflow, 'Proxy Design Pattern: Disadvantages' - Community discussion of Proxy pitfalls: black-box behaviour, lifecycle/state masking and remote proxy concealment. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18302183/proxy-design-pattern-disadvantages

Stack Overflow, 'Performance cost of Java dynamic proxy' - Discusses JDK dynamic proxy overhead, JIT inlining impact and benchmarks, with references to Brian Goetz and Remi Forax's analysis. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1856242/proxy-design-pattern-performance-overhead-of-dynamic-proxies

microservices.io, 'Circuit Breaker Pattern' - Describes the Circuit Breaker as a reliability proxy wrapping remote calls; proxy trips on consecutive failures to prevent cascading outages. https://microservices.io/patterns/reliability/circuit-breaker.html

microservices.io, 'API Gateway / Backends for Frontends Pattern' - API Gateway as a Proxy-based single entry point routing, authenticating and aggregating microservices requests. https://microservices.io/patterns/apigateway.html

NIST SP 800-233, 'Service Mesh Proxy Models for Cloud-Native Applications' - NIST analysis of data-plane proxy architectures (sidecar, node-wide, L4/L7 split) used by service meshes; covers security threat profiles, performance trade-offs and practical guidance for Istio, Linkerd and Consul Connect. https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-233.pdf

Design Patterns in Action, 'Proxy Design Pattern' - Language-agnostic guide with Python/TypeScript/Java/C# examples covering common mistakes, anti-patterns, best practices and thread-safe lazy initialization. https://designpatternsinaction.com/pattern/proxy

TheLinuxCode, 'Proxy Design Pattern: A Practical, Production-Focused Guide' - Production-focused guide covering caching anti-patterns, timeout stacking, proxy recursion, schema drift, cache stampedes and mitigation strategies for remote and cloud-native proxies. https://thelinuxcode.com/proxy-design-pattern-a-practical-production-focused-guide/

GeeksforGeeks, 'Difference Between the Facade, Proxy, Adapter and Decorator Design Patterns' - Clear intent-based heuristic distinguishing Proxy (access control), Decorator (dynamic behaviour), Adapter (interface compatibility) and Facade (simplified subsystem interface). https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/difference-between-the-facade-proxy-adapter-and-decorator-design-patterns/

Python.org Discussion, 'Typing support for common proxy and delegation patterns' - Community discussion (2024) exploring proposals for @delegates decorator, Proxy[T] magic superclass and generic support for Python typing to express delegation patterns statically. https://discuss.python.org/t/typing-support-for-common-proxy-and-delegation-patterns/77909

Stack Overflow, 'Python proxy class with type hints' - Discusses using typing.Protocol with __getattr__-based proxies and solutions for static type checker visibility of dynamically forwarded methods. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/77824044/python-proxy-class-with-type-hints

Thinking in Python, 'Surrogate' - In-depth Python-specific treatment of __getattr__ delegation, __getattribute__ vs __getattr__, name mangling, type checking implications and practical guidance for building Pythonic surrogates. https://thinkinginpython.com/26_Surrogate.html

Douglas Schmidt, 'POSA2' - Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Volume 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (Schmidt et al.) - Covers Proxy variants for distributed systems including remote, virtual, protection and smart reference proxies with ACE framework examples.

GoF Proxy chapter (online excerpt) - Defines Proxy as a surrogate/placeholder with the same interface used to control access, including remote, virtual and protection variants. https://flylib.com/books/en/2.505.1.20/1/

Oracle, 'InvocationHandler' - Official Java SE API documentation describing dispatch, return-type compatibility and checked-exception behavior for dynamic proxies. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/reflect/InvocationHandler.html

Hibernate ORM, 'org.hibernate.proxy package summary' - Official Javadocs documenting the lazy-loading proxy SPI and its LazyInitializer/ProxyFactory components. https://docs.hibernate.org/orm/current/javadocs/org/hibernate/proxy/package-summary.html

Istio, 'Architecture' - Official documentation describing Envoy sidecar proxies as the data plane that mediates traffic, telemetry and policy for workloads. https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/deployment/architecture/

Xebia, 'The Problem With Proxy-based AOP Frameworks' - Criticism documenting how self-invocation bypasses proxy advice, a concrete misuse/limitation of proxy-based interception. https://xebia.com/blog/the-problem-with-proxy-based-aop-frameworks/
